cases.title: Ecuador July 2025 public worker dismissals
cases.point: Quito, seat of the national government and its ministries (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ecuador has had a 48-month Extended Fund Facility since May 2024. In July 2025 the IMF raised it from US$4 billion to US$5 billion. The program's fiscal plan counts on cutting the public wage bill by 1.2% of GDP over 2024-2028 (IMF Country Report 25/199). No published IMF condition names dismissals or ministry mergers.

cases.conditions: IMF Country Report 25/199 (July 2025, second review) lists wages and salaries as the largest spending item in the program's fiscal adjustment: 0.2% of GDP a year in 2024-2026 and 0.3% in 2027-2028, 1.2% of GDP in total. The report contains no structural benchmark or performance criterion on public jobs. In the government's own policy memorandum to the IMF (Country Report 25/341, December 2025), under 'Public Sector Wage Bill', the authorities write that 'in June 2025, we streamlined ministries and other public agencies' and plan to keep limiting headcount and wages.
cases.community: On 24 July 2025 government spokesperson Carolina Jaramillo announced that 5,000 public servants in administrative posts in ministries and the social security institute (IESS) would be dismissed; police, health staff and teachers were excluded. Notices began arriving on 25 July (Bloomberg Línea). The executive went from 20 to 14 ministries: Culture, Sports and Higher Education were merged into Education; Environment into Energy; Women and Human Rights into Government (Peoples Dispatch). Prensa Latina reports a 41% cut in ministries and secretariats. Ecuador had 490,496 public servants (Labour Minister Ivonne Núñez). An analyst at the Observatorio de Política Fiscal estimated savings of under US$50 million a year. Economist Pablo Dávalos estimated that the full 1.2%-of-GDP wage cut would mean about 70,000 public job losses by 2028.
cases.outcome: On 25 July 2025 feminist, artist and cultural groups protested in Quito against the mergers. The FUT union federation and the teachers' union UNE asked the Constitutional Court to review the decision; six unconstitutionality suits were filed by citizens, university unions, judges and prosecutors (Peoples Dispatch). In December 2025 the government told the IMF the June 2025 streamlining was part of its wage bill effort (IMF Country Report 25/341).

cases.confidence_note: The government says the cuts were about efficiency, not IMF demands (spokesperson Jaramillo, via Prensa Latina). FUT president Edwin Bedoya said the new IMF money would be used to fire public sector workers, and opposition legislators Virgilio Hernández and Viviana Veloz called the dismissals IMF commitments (Prensa Latina). The IMF documents set an overall wage bill cut (1.2% of GDP by 2028) but name no dismissals; the government's December 2025 memorandum to the IMF lists the June 2025 ministry streamlining under wage bill containment. Bloomberg Línea calls the restructuring 'also related' to IMF commitments.

cases.title: Mongolia 2017 IMF program: pay freeze, retirement age and child money cut
cases.point: Sukhbaatar Square, site of the January 2018 union rally

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year Extended Fund Facility agreed February 2017 and approved 24 May 2017. Prior action: passing the 2017 supplementary budget with the fiscal measures needed for program targets (IMF Country Report 17/140).

cases.conditions: IMF Country Report 17/140 (May 2017) lists the program's fiscal measures: containing the public wage bill (1.4% of GDP), reforming public pensions (1.5% of GDP over 2017-2019), raising social security contributions (0.6% of GDP), partly reversing a cut in fuel excise (0.8% of GDP), a progressive income tax (0.2% of GDP), and targeting the Child Money Program to the poorest households. IMF Country Report 17/396 (December 2017) says the 2018 budget adds another year of the public wage and hiring freeze, raises the retirement age (to 65 for men by 2027 and for women by 2037, from 60 and 55), raises the social contribution rate, and limits Child Money to the poorest 60% of children; that targeting was a structural benchmark due end-December 2017.
cases.community: Civil servants' pay was frozen; the IMF notes protests by doctors and teachers (Country Report 17/396). Limiting Child Money to the poorest 60% of children removed the benefit from the other 40% (IMF Country Report 17/396). The UB Post reports that a study found the higher personal income tax hit 11.7% of the population, against 8% expected, and that 1,461 people petitioned parliament against it. Teachers had sought pay rises since August 2017 without result.
cases.outcome: In April 2017 the IMF resident representative told the Confederation of Mongolian Trade Unions that Mongolia had 'no choice' but to raise the retirement age gradually (GoGo Mongolia). On 12 January 2018 more than 10,000 people joined a peaceful CMTU rally in Sukhbaatar Square against the retirement age rise and seven tax increases (UB Post; CIVICUS Monitor); the union threatened strikes and rallies in every province.

cases.title: Nicaragua: closure of the farm development bank BANADES
cases.point: Managua, seat of BANADES (approximate); its branches were spread across rural Nicaragua

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The 1994-97 ESAF barred new state recapitalisation of BANADES and new central bank financing of state banks (Policy Framework Paper 1994-97). For the 1998 ESAF the IMF demanded that BANADES be closed or privatized; the government's Letter of Intent pledged to cancel its banking licence (Envío, Feb 1998).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Co-author of the 1994-97 Policy Framework Paper. With the IDB, financed the US$50 million downsizing of BANADES (Envío, Sept 1997).

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank
lenders.role: Supported the BANADES restructuring: fewer staff and branches (Policy Framework Paper 1994-97).

cases.conditions: ESAF Policy Framework Paper 1994-97 (prepared with IMF and World Bank staff): restructure BANADES with fewer staff and branches; no new government recapitalisation of BANADES or BANIC; no net central bank financing of state banks from 1994; no directed credit. Under the 1998-2002 ESAF the National Development Bank had to be liquidated to at least 80% of its assets (Acevedo, Envío 2008).
cases.community: Funding for BANADES was cut in 1992; its branches fell from 117 to 71 and hundreds of staff were laid off. State banks' share of net credit fell from 83% (1992) to 14% (June 1997) (Superintendency of Banks, via Envío). Agriculture's share of credit fell from 30% (1991) to about half that in 1996. A Nitlapán study found 62% of small and medium rural producers still had no credit in 1995; coffee growers' group UNICAFE found banks lent only 19% of the credit coffee producers needed in 1997; moneylenders charged 10-20% a month (Envío, Jan 1998). In 1997 the plan was to sell 42 of 57 remaining branches and lay off about 1,000 staff (Envío, Sept 1997).
cases.outcome: President Alemán had campaigned to recapitalise BANADES and reopen rural branches, then signed a 1998 Letter of Intent pledging to cancel its licence. He proposed a state institute for poor farmers on what remained (Envío, Feb 1998). Acevedo (2008) writes that rural credit programs and institutions for small producers were dismantled.

cases.title: Nicaragua public pay freeze and job cuts under ESAF

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: ESAF 1994-97 and ESAF/PRGF 1998-2002. A real-terms payroll freeze later became a performance criterion (Acevedo, Envío 2008).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Co-prepared the 1994-97 Policy Framework Paper that set the job cut targets.

cases.conditions: Policy Framework Paper 1994-97: cut public employees by 13,500 (about 13%) by end-1996 (7,000 by end-1994, 11,000 by end-1995), described as voluntary; cut about 600 more military posts; freeze public wages and salaries except for a small group; 'cost recovery' fees for secondary schools (per Acevedo). The 1998-2002 ESAF required cutting state employment by a further 15,500 (Acevedo, Envío 2008). In 1997 the IMF proposed 10,000 public layoffs and rejected the government's offer of 3,000 (Envío, Sept 1997).
cases.community: Average public worker pay fell from US$140 to US$93 a month between 1992 and 1997, from 74% to 54% of the national average wage; total public salary spending fell from US$157 million to US$105 million (Treasury Ministry Public Function Division, via Acevedo). Teachers' real take-home pay was about half the national average (Acevedo). Electricity, water and phone rates were raised (Envío, Sept 1997).
cases.outcome: The 1998 Letter of Intent planned about 3,000 more public job cuts, with more expected from privatizations (Envío, Feb 1998). Acevedo (2008) concludes that five IMF agreements over sixteen years did not lift Nicaragua out of poverty.

cases.title: Honduras 1990 adjustment package (Callejas)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Bank waived and released the frozen second tranche of SAL I in June 1990, citing the package (including public job cuts and tariff cuts) as meeting and exceeding its conditions; SAL II followed (World Bank Performance Audit Report, 1996).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Sent a mission in February 1990 alongside the World Bank and IDB; Honduras signed its first IMF stand-by in over a decade in July 1990 (World Bank Performance Audit Report).

cases.conditions: World Bank Performance Audit Report on SAL I, SAL II and the SAC (1996): after parallel Bank, IMF and IDB missions in February 1990, the government announced a 50% devaluation, a revenue rise of 5% of GDP through large public utility tariff increases and taxes, dismissal of 6,000 public employees, import tariff cuts from 90% to 40%, higher interest rate ceilings, and the end of most price controls. The Bank's June 1990 waiver request said these measures 'fundamentally complied with, and in many cases exceeded' SAL I second-tranche conditions.
cases.community: 6,000 public employees dismissed. Consumer prices rose 23.3% in 1990 and 34% in 1991. The real national wage index fell from 100 (1989) to 87.6 (1991). The World Bank notes a significant rise in poverty in 1990 and real per capita income fell slightly over 1990-95 (World Bank Performance Audit Report, using Bank poverty assessment data).
cases.killed_note: No deaths recorded in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The Bank's evaluators judged that the measures laid the groundwork for recovery, but found unemployment, underemployment and poverty stayed around 30% of the labour force through 1990-95 and that Honduras missed IMF stand-by targets from September 1990.

sources.title: Honduras: First and Second Structural Adjustment Loans and Structural Adjustment Credit, Performance Audit Report

cases.confidence_note: The link rests on the World Bank's own evaluation, which treats the package as fulfilling its loan conditions. The only source is the Bank itself; no independent count of the 6,000 dismissals or of protests was found.

cases.title: Honduras Agricultural Modernization Law and reform land sales
cases.point: Lower Aguán Valley near Tocoa, where most reform-sector land sales took place (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Agricultural Sector Adjustment Credit (AGSAC), US$60 million, July 1993. Enacting Law 31-92 with 'satisfactory' land tenure changes was an action required before the credit went to the Board; tranche releases depended on a Land Tenure Action Plan and on divesting the farm bank BANADESA. SAL II (1990) set the first BANADESA restructuring.

lenders.name: USAID
lenders.role: Merlet (2002) says the law was defined mainly with USAID advisers as part of structural adjustment.

cases.conditions: World Bank President's Report P-5923-HO (1993), para. 102: before Board presentation, Law 31-92 (Agricultural Modernization Law, April 1992) with 'satisfactory modifications to the land tenure and forestry policies' had to be enacted and its regulations approved. The law legalised land rental, let reform beneficiaries take individual titles and sell land, dropped the 5-hectare minimum for titles, and ended tenancy as grounds for expropriation. Second and third tranches required divesting BANADESA, the main formal lender to small farmers, and capping its central bank funding at the August 1991 level. Under SAL II, IHMA's grain silos were privatized and guaranteed grain prices replaced by a price band.
cases.community: By May 1994 reform-sector farmer groups had sold more than 30,000 ha, just over 7% of reformed land, over 80% of it on the north coast (Merlet, 2002). Within a few years of the law, three large landowners held over three-quarters of arable land in the Lower Aguán; some cooperative leaders sold land without members' consent, and landowners used threats and violence to press sales (Holland, Carnegie Council, 2014). BANADESA laid off 45% of its staff under the SAL II plan (World Bank, 1993); the Bank's later audit says one-third.
cases.suppression: Holland (2014) reports landowners used 'trickery, threats, harassment, and violence' to press cooperative members to sell. The later Aguán killings (from 2009) are mapped as a separate case.
cases.killed_note: No deaths counted for 1992-1994 in the sources used; Human Rights Watch's count of 92 killings in the Lower Aguán relates to the post-2009 conflict, mapped separately.
cases.outcome: Merlet (2002) writes that gains from land reform were 'seriously undermined' within a few years and that new land struggles with violence and repression emerged, especially in the north. Promised settlement aid and land fund mechanisms were not put in place. The Lower Aguán land conflict later became one of the deadliest in Central America.
